Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

questions.question: Should we key the rate limit on the existing `x-customer-id` request header?

options.label: Yes — `x-customer-id`
options.tradeoff: Fair per-customer enforcement and natural enterprise-tier mapping; requires every caller to send the header or we need a fallback rule.
options.description: Recommended: identifies the business entity, not the network path.

options.label: No — client IP
options.tradeoff: Simpler to extract but breaks when multiple customers share a NAT/proxy and cannot distinguish enterprise tiers.
options.description: Key on TCP/client IP address.

options.label: No — both with precedence
options.tradeoff: Covers headerless callers but adds complexity and ambiguous cases when IP and header disagree.
options.description: Use `x-customer-id` when present, fall back to IP.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists three possible keys: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
brief.what: The key determines whose burst we throttle and whether enterprise tiers can have different limits.
brief.how: If you accept `x-customer-id`, the next round asks whether to require it or fall back. If you choose IP, enterprise tiering becomes an IP-mapping problem.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm for the rate limit?

options.label: Yes — token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows scripted bursts up to a bucket size while capping sustained rate; more implementation effort than fixed window.
options.description: Recommended: smooth, burst-tolerant behavior.

options.label: No — fixed window
options.tradeoff: Easy to implement but creates a thundering-herd spike at each window boundary and penalizes traffic near edges.
options.description: Count requests in fixed time windows.

options.label: No — sliding window
options.tradeoff: More precise than fixed window but needs more Redis operations and bookkeeping for this week's ship date.
options.description: Track each request timestamp over a rolling interval.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
brief.what: The algorithm controls burst shape and how enterprise scripts experience the limit.
brief.how: Token bucket pairs naturally with enterprise burst allowances; fixed/sliding window make burst definitions sharper.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster?

options.label: Yes — Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Shared state across the 3 server instances gives consistent enforcement; adds a runtime dependency and failover behavior to decide.
options.description: Recommended: reuse existing Redis cluster used for sessions.

options.label: No — in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: No external dependency and simpler code, but each instance enforces its own limit and total capacity varies with routing.
options.description: Store counters locally in each `src/server.ts` process.

options.label: No — hybrid local cache + Redis
options.tradeoff: Reduces Redis load but adds synchronization complexity and consistency edge cases; likely too much for this week.
options.description: Local counters flushed to Redis.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes 3 instances behind a load balancer and an existing Redis 7 cluster used by another service.
brief.what: Counter location determines whether enforcement is instance-local or cluster-wide, and whether Redis unreachability matters.
brief.how: If you choose Redis, the next round asks fail-open vs fail-closed. If you choose in-memory, rollout and enterprise limits need per-instance capacity math.

questions.question: Should engineering own per-customer limits, looked up by `x-customer-id`, with sales/product requesting changes via ticket?

options.label: Yes — engineering-owned config
options.tradeoff: Shippable this week and auditable; puts ongoing limit changes on engineering until a self-serve tool is built.
options.description: Recommended: config stored in env/Postgres/Redis, applied by customer ID.

options.label: No — self-serve portal owned by sales/product
options.tradeoff: Scales better long-term but is a separate product feature that will not ship this week.
options.description: Build an admin UI for setting limits.

options.label: No — clients self-declare via header
options.tradeoff: Fastest to implement but any client can claim enterprise tier; needs cryptographic proof to be safe.
options.description: Use `x-rate-limit-tier` sent by clients.

options.label: No — same limit for everyone
options.tradeoff: Simplest but will break the ~20 enterprise integrations that legitimately burst.
options.description: Single global limit.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks how enterprise customers get higher limits and who owns those numbers.
brief.what: This defines the configuration surface, who can change limits, and how an enterprise customer is identified.
brief.how: This decision directly determines the rollout strategy and what a rejected enterprise client sees.

questions.question: Should a rejected request receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a JSON error body?

options.label: Yes — 429 + Retry-After + JSON body
options.tradeoff: Standard, machine-readable for scripts, and gives callers what they need to back off; requires agreeing on body schema.
options.description: Recommended: { error, retry_after, limit, window }.

options.label: No — 429 with plain text only
options.tradeoff: Easy to implement but scripts must parse the text, and we cannot communicate tier-specific guidance cleanly.
options.description: Plain text error message.

options.label: No — 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Misleading status;Retry-After is still valid with 503, but 429 is the correct semantic for rate limiting.
options.description: Return 503 instead of 429.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks what a rejected client sees.
brief.what: The response format determines how automated integrations react and whether customers know how to fix their behavior.
brief.how: This decision feeds into the implementation of the middleware and any customer communications.

questions.question: Should we key the rate limit on the existing `x-customer-id` request header?

options.label: Yes — `x-customer-id`
options.tradeoff: Fair per-customer enforcement and natural enterprise-tier mapping; requires every caller to send the header or we need a fallback rule.
options.description: Recommended: identifies the business entity, not the network path.

options.label: No — client IP
options.tradeoff: Simpler to extract but breaks when multiple customers share a NAT/proxy and cannot distinguish enterprise tiers.
options.description: Key on TCP/client IP address.

options.label: No — both with precedence
options.tradeoff: Covers headerless callers but adds complexity and ambiguous cases when IP and header disagree.
options.description: Use `x-customer-id` when present, fall back to IP.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists three possible keys: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
brief.what: The key determines whose burst we throttle and whether enterprise tiers can have different limits.
brief.how: If you accept `x-customer-id`, the next round asks whether to require it or fall back. If you choose IP, enterprise tiering becomes an IP-mapping problem.

questions.question: Should we use a token-bucket algorithm for the rate limit?

options.label: Yes — token bucket
options.tradeoff: Allows scripted bursts up to a bucket size while capping sustained rate; more implementation effort than fixed window.
options.description: Recommended: smooth, burst-tolerant behavior.

options.label: No — fixed window
options.tradeoff: Easy to implement but creates a thundering-herd spike at each window boundary and penalizes traffic near edges.
options.description: Count requests in fixed time windows.

options.label: No — sliding window
options.tradeoff: More precise than fixed window but needs more Redis operations and bookkeeping for this week's ship date.
options.description: Track each request timestamp over a rolling interval.

brief.where: PLAN.md lists fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
brief.what: The algorithm controls burst shape and how enterprise scripts experience the limit.
brief.how: Token bucket pairs naturally with enterprise burst allowances; fixed/sliding window make burst definitions sharper.

questions.question: Should counters live in the existing Redis 7 cluster?

options.label: Yes — Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Shared state across the 3 server instances gives consistent enforcement; adds a runtime dependency and failover behavior to decide.
options.description: Recommended: reuse existing Redis cluster used for sessions.

options.label: No — in-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: No external dependency and simpler code, but each instance enforces its own limit and total capacity varies with routing.
options.description: Store counters locally in each `src/server.ts` process.

options.label: No — hybrid local cache + Redis
options.tradeoff: Reduces Redis load but adds synchronization complexity and consistency edge cases; likely too much for this week.
options.description: Local counters flushed to Redis.

brief.where: PLAN.md notes 3 instances behind a load balancer and an existing Redis 7 cluster used by another service.
brief.what: Counter location determines whether enforcement is instance-local or cluster-wide, and whether Redis unreachability matters.
brief.how: If you choose Redis, the next round asks fail-open vs fail-closed. If you choose in-memory, rollout and enterprise limits need per-instance capacity math.

questions.question: Should engineering own per-customer limits, looked up by `x-customer-id`, with sales/product requesting changes via ticket?

options.label: Yes — engineering-owned config
options.tradeoff: Shippable this week and auditable; puts ongoing limit changes on engineering until a self-serve tool is built.
options.description: Recommended: config stored in env/Postgres/Redis, applied by customer ID.

options.label: No — self-serve portal owned by sales/product
options.tradeoff: Scales better long-term but is a separate product feature that will not ship this week.
options.description: Build an admin UI for setting limits.

options.label: No — clients self-declare via header
options.tradeoff: Fastest to implement but any client can claim enterprise tier; needs cryptographic proof to be safe.
options.description: Use `x-rate-limit-tier` sent by clients.

options.label: No — same limit for everyone
options.tradeoff: Simplest but will break the ~20 enterprise integrations that legitimately burst.
options.description: Single global limit.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks how enterprise customers get higher limits and who owns those numbers.
brief.what: This defines the configuration surface, who can change limits, and how an enterprise customer is identified.
brief.how: This decision directly determines the rollout strategy and what a rejected enterprise client sees.

questions.question: Should a rejected request receive HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a JSON error body?

options.label: Yes — 429 + Retry-After + JSON body
options.tradeoff: Standard, machine-readable for scripts, and gives callers what they need to back off; requires agreeing on body schema.
options.description: Recommended: { error, retry_after, limit, window }.

options.label: No — 429 with plain text only
options.tradeoff: Easy to implement but scripts must parse the text, and we cannot communicate tier-specific guidance cleanly.
options.description: Plain text error message.

options.label: No — 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Misleading status;Retry-After is still valid with 503, but 429 is the correct semantic for rate limiting.
options.description: Return 503 instead of 429.

brief.where: PLAN.md asks what a rejected client sees.
brief.what: The response format determines how automated integrations react and whether customers know how to fix their behavior.
brief.how: This decision feeds into the implementation of the middleware and any customer communications.
